stories.title: CPSC Issues Safety Warning on bblüv Grow High Chair — Stop Use Immediately

x_posts.label: Post 1-1
x_posts.text: SAFETY WARNING: Stop using the bblüv Grow high chair. CPSC issued a warning — the restraint system isn't factory-assembled, creating serious fall and entrapment risk. Dispose of it now. #COSParenting #ColoradoSprings #COSKids #PikesPeakParenting

x_posts.label: Post 1-2
x_posts.text: Own a bblüv Grow high chair? CPSC says the restraint system was never assembled at the factory — serious fall and entrapment risk for your child. Stop use now. Check cpsc.gov for next steps. #COSParenting #ColoradoSprings #COSKids #PikesPeakParenting

facebook.long_form:
If you own the bblüv Grow high chair, the CPSC wants you to stop using it right now.

On October 15, 2026, the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission issued Warning #27-031 against the bblüv Grow high chair. The hazard is specific: the restraint system was never assembled during manufacturing. That means the straps meant to keep your child secured in the seat weren't functional — creating serious fall and entrapment risks for any child using the chair.

Here's the part that matters: this isn't a typical recall. bblüv Group declined to cooperate with a corrective action plan, so CPSC issued a unilateral warning instead. No injuries had been confirmed at the time of the warning, but that's exactly why the CPSC acts before someone gets hurt.

The directive from CPSC is clear: stop using it, don't sell it, don't give it away, and dispose of it. If you purchased the chair from a third-party online seller (it was sold through various online platforms), you may want to contact your retailer about a refund, and you can check cpsc.gov for any remedy updates.

If you know anyone who has this high chair — especially new parents, grandparents, or caregivers — share this post.

Have you ever received a product recall or warning for something your family uses regularly?

stories.title: Apple and AAP Team Up on Free Screen Time Guide for Families

x_posts.label: Post 2
x_posts.text: Apple and the AAP released a free 6-step guide for families managing kids' screen time — from Child Accounts to device schedules. Worth a read at apple.com #COSParenting #ColoradoSprings #COSKids #PikesPeakParenting

facebook.long_form:
If you've ever looked at your kid's screen time report and just felt defeated — Apple and the American Academy of Pediatrics have something for you.

On September 29, 2026, they released a free joint guide: "Building Healthy Digital Habits: A Guide for Families." It's six practical steps that walk parents through the actual tools inside iOS 27, informed by the AAP's current guidance on kids and screens.

Here's the short version:

1. Start a conversation about screen time — before the devices, before the rules.
2. Set up a Child Account, which gives your child age-appropriate access and keeps things within your control.
3. Use Ask to Buy and Ask to Browse to approve apps and websites before kids access them.
4. Build a device schedule — daily time allowances and specific off times (homework, dinner, sleep).
5. Manage communication — decide who your child can call, message, and FaceTime.
6. Revisit the plan as your child grows — what works at age 8 doesn't work at age 13.

The AAP dropped the old two-hour limit for school-age children in early 2026. Their current focus is on quality over quantity — is the content educational, is a parent nearby, is it replacing sleep or exercise? The guide weaves that thinking into every step.

It's free, it's practical, and it lives at apple.com. Worth spending 15 minutes with this week.

What's your family's screen time situation these days?

---

stories.title: D11 and D49 Fall Break Ends Tonight — Schools Are Back Monday

x_posts.label: Post 3
x_posts.text: D11 and D49 families — fall break ends today. Schools are back tomorrow, Monday Oct. 26. Tonight's checklist: backpack packed, lunches set, bedtime back on track. You've got this. #COSParenting #ColoradoSprings #COSKids #PikesPeakParenting

facebook.long_form:
For D11 and D49 families: today's the last day of fall break. Schools are back tomorrow, Monday, October 26.

D11's break ran October 19–23. D49's ran October 13–23. Both districts resume Monday morning. If you're in D20, your district was on a different schedule — you're likely already back.

Sunday nights after a school break can feel like a scramble. A few things worth doing before bed tonight:

Pack the backpack now, not at 7:15 tomorrow morning. If your child's water bottle, folders, or library books were home during break, get them back in the bag tonight.

Check the lunch situation. Is there food in the house for tomorrow? Is your child doing hot lunch or cold? A five-minute check prevents morning chaos.

Reset the bedtime. A week of staying up late means tired kids tomorrow. Getting to bed 30–45 minutes earlier than your kids want to tonight is worth the argument.

Mention it in passing. Some kids do better with a heads-up: "Hey, school starts again tomorrow — we're going to do dinner early and wind down by 8:30." It's not a big deal, but it helps.

D20 and charter families — hope you've had a smooth week. And to everyone going back tomorrow: it's almost November. You've got this.

x_posts.text: Halloween week in COS 🎃 Fleet Feet Fun Run, Oct. 30 at 6 PM (free, Palmer Park). SoccerHaus Indoor Festival, Oct. 31, 2–8 PM (free). Venetucci Farm open today 9:30 AM–4 PM. Verify times before you go. #COSParenting #ColoradoSprings #COSKids #PikesPeakParenting

facebook.long_form:
There are still six days until Halloween, and COS has a few more family events on the calendar before October 31.

Tonight is also one of the final opportunities at Venetucci Farm (5210 S US Hwy 85-87), which has been running its fall harvest weekends through the end of October. Hours are 9:30 AM–4 PM. It's a classic Colorado Springs fall tradition — pumpkins in the field, a low-key family atmosphere, and a chance to get outside before the cold fully sets in. Worth verifying their 2026 hours at venetuccifarm.org before you head out.

Looking ahead in the week: Fleet Feet is hosting a Halloween Fun Run on Thursday, October 30, starting at 6 PM. It's a free 5K to Palmer Park — kid-friendly, dog-friendly, costumes encouraged, prizes for best costume. A good one for older kids who want to do something active before Halloween.

Then on October 31 itself, the SoccerHaus Indoor Family Halloween Festival is an option if the weather turns or your family wants an indoor celebration. SoccerHaus (4845 List Drive) runs the event from 2 PM to 8 PM — typically free, with bounce houses, treat stations, face painting, a photo booth, and a sensory-friendly hour from 2:30–3:30 PM. The event benefits Aedyn's Backpack Club, organized by Connecting Communities. Verify at connectingcommunities.co or on their Facebook page before going.

For the remaining family events listings, Colorado Springs also has its own parks and rec calendar at coloradosprings.gov/parks.

stories.title: Halloween Night Safety — Last-Week Checklist for COS Families

x_posts.label: Post 5
x_posts.text: Halloween is 6 days away. Children's pedestrian risk is 43% higher that night (Safe Kids). CSPD: kids under 12 need adult supervision. Tip: reflective tape and a flashlight go a long way. Stay safe, COS. #COSParenting #ColoradoSprings #COSKids #PikesPeakParenting

facebook.long_form:
Halloween is six days away, which means it's time for the safety prep checklist.

The numbers matter here: child pedestrian fatality risk is statistically about 43% higher on Halloween night than on comparable fall evenings, according to Safe Kids Worldwide. It's not about stranger danger — that's largely a myth. It's about the combination of dark streets, excited kids, distracted drivers, and costumes that aren't designed with visibility in mind.

A few things that actually help:

Reflective tape on costumes goes a long way. A strip on a bag, a jacket, a shoe — it doesn't have to be visible in daylight to matter in the dark.

Flashlights and glow sticks serve double duty: they help drivers see your kids, and they help your kids see. Grab them before you go.

Skip the full-face masks. If your child's costume includes one, consider swapping it for face paint. Full masks reduce peripheral vision and make it harder to see curbs, cars, and other hazards.

CSPD recommends that children under 12 have adult supervision. The fun run of kids going on their own starts at 12 and up, depending on the neighborhood — use your judgment.

Cross at crosswalks. This sounds obvious, but Halloween excitement means kids will dart into the street. Reinforce this before you leave the house.

The Teal Pumpkin Project: if your family has food allergies, look for homes displaying a teal pumpkin — they're offering non-food treats. FARE (Food Allergy Research & Education) has a map at allergyfamilies.com.

The ideal trick-or-treat window in Colorado Springs is roughly 5:30–8 PM. Wrapping up by 8 keeps the risk window manageable.

What's your family's one non-negotiable Halloween safety rule?
